title: Job
description: Work that should not run in an agent's session, committed and run later by the pipeline (jobs/README.md): a dependency resolution, a build, a test run, a proof, a maintenance task. The pipeline owns its identity, its attempts, its scheduling, its budget, its outputs and its record. What a Gradle task, a Maven goal, a test selector or a checker's verdict means belongs to the workload the job names. A job of the first format (verification-job/v1, verification/schema/job.schema.json) is read as it always was.

id.description: UTC submission time and a slug of the title; also the file name. A job made from a batch's manifest takes the batch's time, its name, its row and the first characters of the row's work identity, so that submitting the same manifest again gives the same id.

title.description: One line: what the job does.

description.description: For a reader who did not see the session: what the job does, why it is needed, and anything a reader of the result should know.

purpose.description: What kind of work it is. Kept apart from the labels: a purpose says how to read the result (a resolve job's is a readiness receipt, a test job's is which tests executed, a verify job's is a conclusion about a claim), whatever project or tool it is for.

workload.description: The adapter that knows what the steps mean (jobs/workloads/NAME.py). `generic`, the default, knows nothing: commands, exit codes, outputs. `verification` builds the checker a job requires and reads proof verdicts out of the logs. `resolution` prepares what a named build task needs and proves it suffices offline. A runner without the adapter does not run the job, and says so.

labels.description: What the job is about, for grouping and calibration: `project`, `tool`, `capability` (what the first format called capabilities), or any other key. None of them changes how the job runs.

links.description: What the job is about, by kind: examples (ids), paths (files), commits, jobs (related jobs), urls, claims.

expected.description: What fulfilment looks like, in words. A reader compares the result with this.

case.description: The case the job belongs to, as its batch or brief names it (S48, say).

batch.description: Set for a job made from a manifest (jobs/batch.py): the batch, the row's stable identity in it, and the row's work identity. A row whose revision, task or inputs change has another work identity, and so another job.

work.description: SHA-256 of what the row asks to be done.

session.description: The submitting session, to find the conversation behind the job.

run.description: The run the submitting session was working in (single-NAME), read from the scope the loop runs its agent in. Absent when the job was submitted outside a run. It is not the source revision, and not who collects the result.

phase.description: The phase of that run: generation, setup, domain, or watcher for the watcher's own.

source.description: The commit to run at. Leave it out: the runner takes the last commit that touched the job's file, which is the change the job was written for.

needs.description: What must be there before the job is scheduled. `job`: that job, or one that supersedes it, has a fulfilled result. `readiness`: a readiness receipt with that key is valid on the runner (jobs/readiness.py). A job whose prerequisite is not finished waits; one whose prerequisite ended unfulfilled is blocked, with the reason, and consumes no attempt.

requires.description: What must be on the runner: a command on PATH, or a name the job's workload knows how to look for or to build. A job that requires something the runner lacks is not run there, and says so.

resources.description: A rough estimate. The runner shares its budget out by these numbers, caps the job at its limit, and reports what it used next to them.

fetch.description: How many downloads at once its fetch steps make (a build tool's parallel resolution). Counted against the runner's fetch slots while such a step runs. Default 1.

environment.description: What the steps are permitted beyond the export of the commit.

network.description: The default for every step. `host`: as the runner's machine gives it (what every job of the first format gets). `none`: the step runs in a network namespace with a loopback interface alone, shown by a probe the result keeps; a runner that cannot enforce it does not run the job. `fetch`: the network, for a step of a resolve job on a runner whose settings authorise fetching, counted against the runner's fetch slots.

steps.description: Run in order, each a bash script in a clean export of the job's commit. One command and nothing else is a job.

run.description: A bash script, run with bash -c.

cwd.description: Relative to the repository root. Default '.'.

expectExit.description: The exit code, or codes, that count as the step going as expected. Default 0.

phase.description: What the step's time is counted as: resolve, fetch, prepare, build, test, proof or other.

network.description: This step's network, over the job's default.

promises.description: What the step says it does besides exiting as expected. A promise that is not kept leaves the job unfulfilled, whatever the exit code.

tests.description: The step runs tests. `min`: at least this many must have executed (default 1): a step that compiled and ran none has not kept it. `reports`: where to read what executed, as globs of JUnit XML files relative to the repository root; without it the step's log is read for the summary lines of cargo, unittest, pytest, Maven and Gradle. `failing`: tests expected to fail by assertion, by name: the step's exit code is then its tool's failure code (expectExit), and the promise is kept when exactly these failed and they failed in a test, not in the build.

stopOnFailure.description: Skip the later steps once one does not go as expected. Default true.

outputs.description: Files or directories, relative to the repository root, that the job writes and that should come back. A plain path is required: when the job ends without it the job is not fulfilled, even if every step exited as expected. `required: false` marks one that may be absent.

consumer.description: Who reads it: a job id, a case, a tool.

supersedes.description: The job this one replaces: the same work with other resources, or at a newer commit. A rerun of the same job is an attempt, not a new job.
